title: Performance and Limitations
summary: Connect loading, atmosphere, and aircraft limits to the runway and climb performance you actually need.
objectives: Calculate weight and center of gravity, including changes during flight.
Explain why weight, CG, density altitude, wind, and surface condition change performance.
Read aircraft-specific performance charts with their assumptions and choose a defensible operating margin.

sections.title: Weight and balance: both limits matter
sections.body:
Weight is the total load. Balance describes where that load acts. An airplane can be below maximum weight and still have an unsafe center of gravity (CG). Both must remain inside the aircraft’s approved envelope throughout the planned flight, including after fuel burns.

Use the aircraft’s current equipment list and weight-and-balance record. A sample handbook’s empty weight may differ from your airplane after repairs, equipment changes, or weighing. Basic empty weight normally includes installed equipment, unusable fuel, and operating fluids as defined for that aircraft. Useful load is the difference between the applicable maximum weight and basic empty weight. It must accommodate usable fuel, occupants, and baggage.

Apply it: four seats do not establish a four-person payload. Check total weight, CG, baggage limits, seat limits, and the operating category required for the intended maneuvers.
sections.deep:
Think of CG as a weighted average, rather than a physical hinge. Each item contributes a moment equal to weight multiplied by its arm from the reference datum. Adding moments and dividing by total weight gives the loaded CG. The datum is a bookkeeping reference selected by the manufacturer; the airplane does not rotate around it in flight.

Some manuals scale moments by 100 or 1,000. Keep the same scale throughout. Use the envelope’s actual horizontal axis: it may show inches, percent mean aerodynamic chord, or moment index. A correct arithmetic result plotted on the wrong chart is still an unsafe loading decision.

sections.title: Calculate the effect of moving a load
sections.body:
Build the calculation in a consistent sequence: start with current empty weight and moment, add each load at its assigned arm, sum weights and moments, then divide total moment by total weight. Compare the resulting point with the correct envelope, not just a single maximum-weight number.

For a load shifted within the aircraft, total weight stays constant. The change in moment is the shifted weight multiplied by the distance moved. Divide that moment change by the aircraft’s total weight to find the CG movement.

Worked example: an illustrative 2,000 lb airplane has a CG at 40 in. Moving 100 lb from a 60 in arm to a 100 in arm adds 4,000 lb·in of moment. CG moves 4,000 / 2,000 = 2 in aft, to 42 in. Whether 42 in is acceptable depends entirely on that airplane’s approved envelope.
sections.deep:
For a shift, ΔCG = w × d / W. This shortcut works because the denominator W is unchanged. Adding or removing a load changes both total moment and total weight; recompute both rather than treating it as a shift.

Fuel burn is removal of weight at the tank’s arm. If the tanks lie forward of the current CG, burning their fuel moves CG aft; tanks aft of CG tend to produce the opposite change. Tanks, transfer systems, and loading restrictions vary, so check the actual aircraft and planned fuel states. Secure any approved ballast so its effective arm cannot change during turbulence or maneuvering.

sections.title: Why weight and CG change how the airplane flies
sections.body:
At the same speed and configuration, a heavier airplane needs more lift for level flight. The wing generally operates at a higher angle of attack, leaving less margin to the critical angle. Stall speed increases with the square root of the supported load when configuration and maximum lift coefficient are held fixed.

CG changes stability and control authority as well as performance. In many conventional trainers, a forward CG increases the tail force and wing lift needed for trim, potentially increasing stall speed and drag. Excessively forward loading can leave inadequate elevator authority for rotation or flare. An aft CG reduces longitudinal stability and can worsen stall or spin recovery.

Common trap: a potentially lower stall speed with an aft CG does not make aft-limit loading safer. The approved envelope protects controllability and recovery as well as cruise efficiency.
sections.deep:
For a fixed configuration, stall-speed scaling is VS2 / VS1 = √(W2 / W1) for a 1 g comparison. If weight rises from 2,000 to 2,420 lb, the ratio is √1.21 = 1.10. An illustrative 50 kt reference stall speed becomes 55 kt under the same assumptions.

Maneuvering speed also generally decreases with lower weight. VA is not blanket protection from structural damage: abrupt combined-axis, repeated, or alternating inputs can exceed loads even below it. Use the published weight-dependent speeds and limitations. Stability is properly discussed using pitching moments and the neutral point; the wing’s center of pressure is not a fixed pivot from which the CG simply “falls.”

sections.title: Density altitude connects the atmosphere to performance
sections.body:
Pressure altitude expresses pressure relative to the standard atmosphere and can be read approximately by setting a pressure altimeter to 29.92 inHg. Density altitude is pressure altitude adjusted for nonstandard temperature. Heat, lower pressure, and greater elevation generally raise density altitude; humidity also reduces air density.

Thin air affects the whole system. A normally aspirated engine takes in less oxygen, the propeller accelerates less mass, and the wing needs a higher true airspeed to achieve the same dynamic pressure. Follow the aircraft’s specified indicated takeoff and approach speeds, but expect higher true airspeed at high density altitude. Wind then determines groundspeed.

Apply it: an unchanged runway and familiar indicated rotation speed can still produce a much longer takeoff and weaker climb on a hot afternoon. Evaluate the conditions expected at departure time, not just morning conditions.
sections.deep:
Dynamic pressure is q = ½ρV². Reducing density ρ while holding indicated-air-speed-related dynamic pressure constant requires true airspeed V to increase. This explains why a familiar indicated approach can carry more groundspeed and kinetic energy in thin air when wind is unchanged.

Density altitude is a performance index, not an instruction to add an altitude correction to a flight plan or a universal replacement for chart inputs. If the POH requests pressure altitude and temperature separately, supply those inputs. A pressure-altitude estimate based on field elevation and altimeter setting is an approximation; temperature also affects the relationship between indicated and true altitude.

sections.title: Read the conditions before reading the number
sections.body:
Performance tables answer a specific question under specified conditions. Read the title, units, notes, aircraft weight, pressure altitude, temperature, wind convention, runway condition, configuration, and technique before interpolating. Distinguish ground roll from distance over a specified obstacle.

For takeoff, check both runway distance and the climb needed beyond the runway. A favorable ground roll does not guarantee terrain clearance. For landing, include the approach and obstacle assumptions rather than comparing runway length only with ground roll. Cruise planning needs time, fuel, and distance for climb and descent as well as cruise.

Common trap: copying another trainer’s numbers or extrapolating beyond published chart boundaries. Demonstrate interpolation inside the chart, explain every correction in its notes, and use only approved data applicable to the aircraft and configuration.
sections.deep:
A 500 ft/min climb means 500 vertical feet per minute. Climb gradient asks how many vertical feet are gained per horizontal mile. At 100 kt groundspeed, 500 ft/min corresponds to 500 × 60 / 100 = 300 ft/NM. At 125 kt groundspeed, the same climb rate yields 240 ft/NM. A tailwind can therefore worsen obstacle-clearance geometry even when vertical climb rate is unchanged.

Displayed numbers can look precise while the inputs are uncertain. Ask whether the engine can achieve the charted power, the runway matches the chart condition, and the pilot can consistently achieve the specified technique. If a necessary correction is unavailable, that uncertainty requires a more conservative decision, not invented arithmetic.

sections.title: Make the go/no-go decision before starting the roll
sections.body:
Operating limits and personal margins serve different purposes. Approved weight, CG, speed, and configuration limits must be respected. A personal margin then accounts for uncertainty within those limits: wind shifts, surface condition, pilot technique, aircraft condition, and an escape plan.

A demonstrated crosswind value records a certification demonstration and is often not itself an operating limitation; verify the actual AFM/POH, placards, supplements, school policy, and pilot proficiency. A charted or approved limitation remains a limitation regardless of the label used in a training note.

Apply it: if the plan works only with perfect technique, steady headwind, or optimistic surface assumptions, change the plan. Reduce loading, wait for cooler conditions, choose a different runway or airport, or decline the flight. Decide on aircraft-appropriate abort criteria with your instructor before takeoff.
sections.deep:
There is no universal 10–20% allowance that makes every takeoff, landing, or fuel plan safe. The appropriate margin depends on the aircraft, available data, environment, operation, and consequences of uncertainty. School or operator policies may require defined margins above legal or published minima.

Soft or contaminated surfaces can increase rolling resistance, reduce acceleration, and degrade braking. Never assume grass or softness automatically shortens landing distance. Runway slope, wind, obstacles, and braking conditions must be assessed using applicable data. More indicated airspeed than required can substantially increase landing energy because kinetic energy varies with speed squared; carrying excess speed is not a substitute for a sound margin.

teachBack: Use your airplane’s current loading sheet to explain whether a baggage shift changes weight, CG, or both.
Explain why a high-density-altitude takeoff can reach the usual indicated speed later and climb poorly.
Show the notes that make a performance chart applicable, then state what would make you change the plan.
takeaways: Check weight, CG, compartment limits, and category for all relevant fuel states.
Treat performance results as conditional on the inputs, configuration, and technique in the manual.
A legal loading and a book distance are starting points for judgment, not a guarantee of a safe departure.

quiz.question: An illustrative 2,000 lb airplane has 100 lb of baggage moved 40 in aft. Total weight stays constant. How does CG move?
options: 2 in aft
4 in aft
2 in forward
40 in aft
feedback: The added moment is 100 × 40 = 4,000 lb·in; dividing by 2,000 lb moves CG 2 in aft.
A 4 in shift would require 8,000 lb·in of added moment at this total weight.
Moving the load aft adds aft moment, so the CG cannot move forward.
The baggage moves 40 in, but it is only one twentieth of the total weight.
quiz.hint: Use moment change divided by unchanged total weight.

quiz.question: A hot, high airport has no wind. Compared with a low-density-altitude departure at the same weight and configuration, what should a pilot generally expect?
options: A lower true airspeed at the published rotation indication
A higher true airspeed at the same indication and poorer climb
A lower indicated rotation speed to compensate for thin air
An unchanged takeoff distance because indicated speed is unchanged
feedback: Thin air requires a higher true speed for the same dynamic pressure, not a lower one.
The same indicated target can correspond to greater true speed while engine and propeller performance are reduced.
Use the indicated targets and procedure in the aircraft manual; do not invent a density-altitude speed reduction.
The runway distance depends on acceleration and groundspeed as well as the indicated target.
quiz.hint: Consider the wing, propeller, and normally aspirated engine together.

quiz.question: A trainer is much lighter than its maximum weight. What is the best interpretation of its published maneuvering-speed guidance?
options: Use the maximum-weight value at every weight
Any control input is safe below maneuvering speed
Use the applicable lower weight-dependent value and avoid abrupt combined inputs
Increase maneuvering speed because the airplane is more responsive
feedback: The limiting-load relationship changes with weight; use the manual’s weight guidance.
Maneuvering speed does not cover all repeated, reversing, or combined-axis inputs.
Lower weight generally reduces maneuvering speed, and the speed is not all-purpose structural protection.
A lighter airplane can reach its limiting load at a lower speed, so responsiveness does not justify an increase.
quiz.hint: Think about the load-factor increase possible before the wing stalls.

quiz.question: The POH gives 900 ft ground roll and 1,600 ft over a 50 ft obstacle. The runway is 1,200 ft long with a 50 ft obstacle beyond it. Which comparison is meaningful?
options: 1,200 ft versus 900 ft proves the takeoff works
The two published distances can be averaged
Subtract the obstacle height from the runway length
Assess the obstacle-distance data and the actual departure geometry, with margin
feedback: Ground roll alone says nothing sufficient about clearing the obstacle.
The two values answer different questions and must not be averaged.
Subtracting a vertical height from runway length does not evaluate climb geometry.
The obstacle case requires the applicable obstacle-distance and climb analysis, not just the ground roll.
quiz.hint: Match the chart’s question to the runway’s actual limiting condition.

quiz.question: A loading change remains below maximum gross weight but moves CG beyond the aft limit. What is the appropriate conclusion?
options: The loading is unacceptable even though total weight is legal
The loading is acceptable because stall speed may decrease
A little forward trim makes the loading legal
A longer runway removes the CG concern
feedback: The weight and CG limits must both be satisfied for the operation.
Potential performance changes do not override stability and recovery limits.
Trim does not restore compliance with the approved loading envelope.
Runway length cannot correct an out-of-envelope CG.
quiz.hint: Consider controllability and recovery separately from total weight.

quiz.question: A student adds 20% to a dry, paved runway takeoff value and calls the result safe for a soft grass runway. What should the instructor emphasize?
options: Twenty percent is an FAA guarantee for all runways
Grass always improves landing braking, so the same rule works
Use applicable surface data and a margin justified by the operation; the percentage alone is inadequate
A margin is unnecessary if the aircraft is below maximum weight
feedback: No universal percentage guarantees safe performance in every condition.
Soft or contaminated surfaces can degrade braking and must not be assumed beneficial.
The source chart and its corrections must fit the surface; unexplained uncertainty cannot be cured by a generic percentage.
Weight is only one input; runway and environmental conditions still matter.
quiz.hint: First decide whether the original chart applies to that surface.
